cells.tense: The cycle is closing and you are the one who gets to say so.
cells.ask: Name one thing as finished this week — out loud, to someone — and leave the next thing unnamed for a day.
cells.core:
You finish things and you stay open at the same time. That's the rare part. Most people either hold on past the end or cut and run before it. A thing closes and you're still available to what comes next — not bracing, not clinging.

What makes that work is that you're choosing it. The this-not-that is coming from you, not from fatigue or from someone else's deadline. So the ending reads as a beginning and not a loss. That's not a trick you learned. It's the shape you're standing in right now.

If you want to keep it, don't get precious about it. The balance holds when you keep picking one thing to close and letting it stay closed.

cells.verb: Closing a cycle and letting the next one open
cells.place: At the point where you choose what this is for

cells.tense: You are already announcing the end of something you have not finished yet.
cells.ask: Pick the one you've been calling done and do the last unglamorous hour of it — today, before you name anything new.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead is the version where this is finished and you can rest. You're living in that version. So the wrap-up gets written before the work is done, the next thing gets named before this one lands, and the closing keeps arriving before the thing it's closing.

It costs you the part that only comes at the actual end. The last stretch — the unglamorous, quiet bit — gets skipped because you've already moved on in your head. The finishing is real work and you're spending it in advance.

Come back to the part that's still open. Not to slow down. To let the ending be something you did, and not something you announced early.

cells.tense: A door is behind you and you are still standing at it.
cells.ask: Take one unfinished thing that's been sitting there and either finish it this week or name it abandoned — one or the other, not both.
cells.core:
You don't let the cycles close. Everything stays slightly open in case something better comes, or in case closing it would mean admitting it's over. So the seeking continues and nothing quite lands. Not because you can't finish. Because you don't give yourself permission to.

The choice that would end it is small, but it's a choice, and that's the part that isn't happening. You're waiting for the ending to arrive on its own. It doesn't. It's made in a moment by someone deciding this, not that.

So close something. Not the biggest thing you've got — something that's been sitting there a while. Either done or abandoned. Both are a close, and either one hands you back a piece of your own direction.

cells.tense: You are deciding which cycles are over and calling it something that happened to you.
cells.ask: For one thing you've been treating as still open, say out loud which it was — kept going on purpose, or ended on purpose. Then act on what you said.
cells.core:
You're already picking which things end and which keep going, in moments nobody watches. It gets described as timing — as if the ending arrived rather than got decided. Underneath, a choice was made. Saying so out loud isn't happening.

That gap leaves you unsure whether a thing is over. The completed ones and the ones you stopped looking at feel the same.

So own one of them. Not the theory of owning. One plain sentence, spoken once, naming one thing as kept or ended by your own hand. That doesn't decide anything for you. It just puts the pen back in your hand where it was the whole time.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say whether this person treats completion as something they owe or something they avoid, so the Too Little cell locates the pattern only as far back as the present door they're still standing at, without naming what happened there. A reader could reasonably say 'I do finish things, I just start the next one before I've called the last one done' — that would move them toward Too Much, not Too Little, and the ask still works from either side because it names a closeable thing, not a feeling. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'each moment is fresh entry' if left abstract, so it stays out of the cells and the ask stays on one visible act.
